Prayers, Shantideva verses, and session 1 structure are assumed to match the prior class (May 3, 2026). The 16 correct/wrong conceptions material covered in session 1 comes from 'How to Understand the Mind' by Geshe Kelsang Gyatso, not from Meaningful to Behold.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and target of remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara’s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma’s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara’s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva’s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the karma path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

shantidevaReading.speaker: Unknown reader
shantidevaReading.note: Not recorded. Assumed same verses as May 3, 2026.
shantidevaReading.text:
(24) To all the Buddhas abiding in the three times,
The Dharma and the Supreme Assembly,
I prostrate with as many emanated bodies
As there are atoms in all the worlds.

(25) I prostrate to the bases for generating bodhichitta,
To the images of Buddha’s body, speech and mind,
To the Abbots and Preceptors,
And to the supreme practitioners on the path.

(26) Until I attain the essence of great enlightenment,
I will go for refuge to the Buddhas;
Likewise, I will go for refuge to Dharma
And to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

(27) With my palms pressed together, I make requests
To those endowed with great compassion —
The perfect Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas
Who abide throughout the ten directions.

(28) Since beginningless time in samsara,
Throughout this and all my previous lives,
Out of ignorance I have committed evil,
Ordered it to be committed,

(29) And, overwhelmed by deceptive ignorance,
Rejoiced in its being committed by others.
Seeing all these to be grave mistakes,
From the depths of my heart I confess them to the holy beings.

(30) Whatever harmful actions of body, speech or mind
I have done under the influence of delusion
Towards the Three Precious Jewels,
My father and mother, my Spiritual Guide, and others —

(31) All the extremely unbearable evil actions
Committed by me, an evil person
Polluted by many faults —
I confess before the Deliverers, the enlightened beings.

(32) But I might die before I purify
All my negativities;
O please protect me so that I
May surely and swiftly be freed from them.

(33) Since the untrustworthy Lord of Death
Will not wait while I purify my evils,
Regardless of whether I am sick or not,
This momentary life is unreliable.

(34) I shall have to leave everything and depart alone
But, through failing to understand this,
I have committed many kinds of evil action
With respect to my friends and others.

(35) And yet my friends will become nothing
And others will also become nothing.
Even I shall become nothing;
Likewise, everything will become nothing.

(36) Just like an experience in a dream,
Everything I now enjoy
Will become a mere recollection,
For what has passed cannot be seen again.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
I can think on my spiritual path, I want to develop understandings that are incontrovertible, that are lasting and stable. I don't want to keep putting work and energy in and having my progress reverse, and then having to do it all over again. I really want to gain Dharma jewels — consistent and stable realizations.

I can think through the sixteen beneficial conceptions and just take one of them and think, what would it be like to have an incontrovertible experience of this mind? With this understanding we can gradually arise from our practice.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
So then it would be nice for us all to kind of keep one of these in mind. I can make sure to send the list out again on the WhatsApp, in case you didn't get it.

But we can keep one of these in mind as we look at the measurement and the commitments of going for refuge. Because the commitments of going for refuge especially are these wonderful practices. They are like twelve facets of refuge, or you could say like twelve mini refuge meditations, that all comprise the kind of greater refuge basket of meditations.

But they are not practiced in abstract — they are best practiced with a target in mind. And so one of the sixteen positive conceptions that we are trying to work on can kind of be funneled into these commitments. And we can see like each one, we can practice with respect to making this positive change in our mind.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: KK recap of unrecorded session 1 and MTB paragraph 330
teaching.text:
So the first half didn't get recorded. So for those who are listening in, this is the first class that you're hearing, even though it's the second class.

Let me try to say what we did in the first class in like one minute. We looked at the section on the sixteen correct conceptual thoughts and the sixteen wrong awarenesses that we try to oppose, from How to Understand the Mind. The idea was that we're on a spiritual path, and on a journey we don't want to take one step forward and one step back. Instead, what we want to do is develop incontrovertible understandings — little realizations. Buddha explains that this is moving from basically not understanding a Dharma object, or having an absolutely wrong understanding, to developing what's called a correct belief in the opposite Dharma understanding, and then turning that into what's called a valid cognizer — which is like a direct understanding that either we can see directly or with a correct reason. It's like proven in our mind, logically proven. When we can do this, then our mind will basically hold these realizations and they won't degrade, and they'll actively oppose the wrong conception that we're trying to let go of.

The sixteen wrong conceptions that we're trying to let go of — these are from page 177 of How to Understand the Mind: disliking or having disrespect for our spiritual guide, not wishing to take the real meaning of our precious human life, not remembering death, being attached to the pleasures and happiness of this life alone, not fearing rebirth in the lower realms, not wishing to go for refuge to the Three Jewels, not having faith or conviction in the laws of karma, seeking to accumulate non-virtuous actions, regarding samsara as having the nature of happiness, wishing to increase delusions and contaminated actions, being uninterested in attaining liberation, not wanting to practice the Three Higher Trainings which are the causes of liberation, forsaking mother living beings, self-cherishing, self-grasping, disliking the practices of secret mantra.

We're looking at these especially in connection to the Five Mahayana Paths — path of accumulation, preparation, seeing, meditation, no more learning. These are high realizations. The first is having tranquil abiding on bodhichitta. So before then, we need to have markers or aims or checkpoints on our spiritual path that are a little bit more approachable. It's nice to take these sixteen, just choose one or two, and make them a focus. In that way, we're really following a path. A spiritual path is like a realization — a deep, lasting insight.

“The true taking of refuge depends upon our clear recognition of the causes mentioned above. Once we have cultivated a dread of various forms of samsaric suffering, and an understanding that only the Three Jewels have the power to protect us from such suffering, from the depths of our heart we will place our full reliance firmly upon Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. When we do this sincerely and consistently, this is the actual going for refuge. To remind us of this and to deepen our refuge, we can recite the following prayer: I go for refuge to the Gurus. I go for refuge to the Buddhas. I go for refuge to the Dharma. I go for refuge to the Sangha.”

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 331–333: commitments and three abandonments
teaching.text:
“Once we have turned to the Three Jewels for refuge, there are a number of commitments we should strive to observe purely. These include three actions to be abandoned, three actions to be acknowledged, and six general commitments.”

“The three abandonments. Once we have taken refuge in the Buddha Jewel, we should abandon going for refuge to teachers who contradict Buddha's view, or to samsaric gods. Having taken refuge in the Dharma Jewel, we should abandon harming others. Having taken refuge in the Sangha Jewel, we should not allow ourselves to be influenced by people who reject Buddha's teachings.”

So we basically take some kind of Dharma jewel we're trying to develop — one of these reversals, like not regarding samsara as the nature of happiness, or just having conviction in the law of karma — and with that as a focus in mind, we can work on practicing these different abandonments, acknowledgements, and general commitments.

For example, with respect to conviction in karma or not regarding samsara as having the nature of happiness — we can think, how is my going for refuge to teachers who contradict Buddha's view, or to samsaric gods, getting in the way of this? It might not be literally people saying karma is not real. But it might be being influenced by teachers or thought leaders through reading their writing, or their philosophy, or their spiritual views, that are actually teaching about finding happiness in samsara and making samsara better. Or not really living in the law of cause and effect. We might even rely on some of these thinkers. So it would be like, I'm not going to rely on thinkers that go against this insight I'm trying to develop.

Abandon harming others — you can link it to either of these. I'm not going to harm others because I'm trying to increase my belief in the law of karma. I'm not going to harm others because they're just suffering, being stuck in the ocean of suffering of samsara. So my practice of abandoning harming others is helping me increase my understanding of this reversal that I'm working on.

Not allowing ourselves to be influenced by people who reject Buddha's teachings — this is a bit more subtle than the first of the three. The first is really taking refuge in a thought leader or teacher who's sending us in the other direction. This is more about not being influenced by people. It's a lot harder to do. It's very easy to be influenced by our friends and family.

How often do people blame bad things or painful experiences on others from their past? All the time. We're just chatting with our friends. 'I'm unhappy because this thing happened to me twenty years ago.' From the Buddha's view, absolutely not. That's not why you're unhappy. It's your karma. It's not because something happened twenty years ago. That's completely wrong.

Are we getting influenced by that view? Maybe we're just trying to be kind, but maybe we're also agreeing internally. We're a little bit ingraining their view into our mind. Even things that are happening in the world — bad things that happen. We say, oh, this is because of them. But it's not. It's because of people's karma. Sometimes you can't say that out loud because it's not a very popular thing to say. And it might not be skillful or kind. But that's the truth. Every bad thing that happens in the world is because of the people's karma who are experiencing that bad thing. Every single one.

We have to be careful not to get into a blaming mindset, pointing fingers on the outside for harm. We can still say, yeah, you need to change, or yeah, what's happening is harmful. But we need to make sure we're not developing a philosophical view thinking the harm is coming from the outside, and that we should blame the outer person.

This one is a little bit subtle. And we'll notice as we try to work on these sixteen, it's very easy to be influenced by others to go in the other direction. We have to be a bit vigilant and thoughtful about this.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
“The three acknowledgements. Having taken refuge in Buddha, we should regard any image of Buddha, whether it is made of gold, wood, or some other material, and regardless of whether it is old or new, as an actual Buddha. Our Dharma refuge requires that we regard any Dharma scripture, even the individual letters, as an actual Dharma Jewel, a Buddha's actual speech. As such, Dharma texts should definitely not be mistreated, placed on the ground, or stepped over. Having taken refuge in the Sangha Jewel, we should regard anyone who wears the robes of an ordained person as an actual Sangha.”

So this is about trying to train in pure view. We can think, how would these three help me change my mind and develop the sixteen positive conceptions? How can I use them practically? Anyone have ideas?

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: Just thinking about the karma one — that it's my karma to be in the presence of this image of Buddha, and realize that it's actually Buddha himself.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. That's so beautiful. It's like, wow, this is my karma. That Buddha's appearing. Past me did something really cool to have this incredibly rare appearance. And it's not just an image of Buddha appearing — it's actually Buddha. That's a lovely way to kind of link them.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Let me read the positive conceptions. Remembering death, wishing to take the real meaning of our precious human life, relying faithfully upon and having respect for our spiritual guide, not being attached to the pleasures and happiness of this life, fearing rebirth in the lower realms, wishing to go for refuge to the Three Jewels, having faith and conviction in the laws of karma, seeking to accumulate virtuous actions and not non-virtuous actions, regarding samsara as having the nature of suffering, wishing to abandon delusions and contaminated actions which are the causes of samsaric rebirth, being determined to attain liberation, wanting to practice the Three Higher Trainings, cherishing all other beings, forsaking self-cherishing, realizing selflessness, liking the practice of secret mantra.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: When you see somebody wearing robes and you regard them as an actual Sangha Jewel, I think that helps you practice tantra. That's almost like a tantric practice — holding pure view for that person. That might make you like the practice more, if you do that.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, for sure. All three of these are leading us in the highest degree into tantra. They're leading us into pure view, which is amazing. Buddha taught these as refuge commitments, even in sutra. But they're really leading people into having pure view, which is so cool. From day one, when you get your refuge vows, you're supposed to learn these commitments and then practice them — like day one. So it's like, wow, Buddha's teaching people how to enter tantra right away.

Another example is wanting to practice the Three Higher Trainings — moral discipline, concentration, and wisdom. We can look at Buddha and think, wow, this is a living Buddha. Look what Buddha did with the Three Higher Trainings. That's so beautiful. And that will spur on this interest to do it ourselves. Or look at the Sangha Jewel — this actual Sangha Jewel. We impute that they realized emptiness directly. We think, wow, I want to do that too.

Like recently, one of Geshe-la's first disciples, Gen Tarchen, died. It was just on Tuesday. He was a monk, one of the first disciples of Geshe-la. He kind of got Manjushri Centre fixed up and put together — he was a carpenter and all that. And then he became a monk. Then he helped set up Tara Centre in Scotland, which is our retreat center. Geshe-la did three years of retreat along with a group of disciples, and Gen Tarchen was part of that.

Then he taught in Toronto and ripened a bunch of monks and nuns and teachers, many of whom are still around today benefiting the whole tradition. Two very long-time teachers and monks in our tradition — they went to their first class with him in Toronto together. They didn't know each other, but they met in the first class. And they were walking home to the train after the first class they ever went to. And one said to the other, I think I want to become a monk. And the other was like, yeah, I do too. And then within a year, they were both monks. This was like 1992 or something. And they're still flourishing Dharma all throughout the world today. It's so beautiful.

Gen Tarchen basically was this incredible meditator. He had so much faith in Geshe-la and incredible concentration. He was known to be like a yogi, like a real meditator yogi. First class, both of them — boom, monks in no time, and then teachers, and then benefiting all over the world.

Then he taught in Tara Centre, Scotland, after Toronto. And then created this retreat center where people go for three months in the snow retreats or just come throughout the year and do a long retreat. Many of the students who either went there on those retreats or who lived there and helped support the center basically help run the whole tradition now, or are some of the most senior teachers in our tradition, through his help.

It's not about idolatry and idolizing this one person. It's just showing the example. He had really strong concentration. And as a result, a lot of faith and experience of Dharma. This is just one person's impact — like a ton of different people.

So just rejoicing in that and looking at that, you go, I want to practice the Three Higher Trainings. You can do that with any Sangha Jewel — just imputing they're like a superior being. But it does help sometimes to have someone like this who you can do this with. You can go, okay, that person maybe feels a little bit more approachable for where I'm at today. But look what they did. That's so beautiful. I can do that too.

His name was Chip before he was Gen Tarchen. He was just a guy — a carpenter and a composer. But he just followed the teachings, really went deeply, changed his life, and then changed a lot of people's lives single-handedly, basically.

teaching.speaker: Mimi
teaching.text: When you see an image of a Buddha, can you also think about your own potential of becoming like a future Buddha? Seeing that that's your pure nature.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 336–338: six general commitments and Atisha
teaching.text:
Yeah, for sure. For example, that would help with the practice of precious human life meditation, or realizing selflessness, or any of the renunciation-based ones. Because you'd be going like, oh, that's like a living Buddha. That's my potential. That's showing me what's inside myself. And then that will naturally evoke that feeling of that meditation.

Okay, we don't need to keep mining these, but I'm just trying to show these aren't just random commitments. These are practices. And the practices are best used when they're targeted at something that we're working on. You can do them in general, of course, and they're incredibly beautiful and delightful. But it's nice to target them at whatever practice we're working on.

We didn't do the Dharma one, but the way you do it is: when you're working on one of those changes, you can pick up a Dharma book, either go to the index if we don't know where to find the teachings on that topic, and you can find it that way, or just go to the pages. But then when you're reading, we're reading with this reverence, thinking this is actual Buddha's speech. This is actually Buddha's speech that we're meeting. And when we have that view, studying and getting the understanding takes a very different form for us. And then it's very blessed and helpful.

“The six general commitments. The following commitments of going for refuge should also be borne in mind throughout life. Each of them is designed to enhance beneficial attitudes and maintain the liberating thought of refuge in the forefront of our consciousness. Thus, we should go for refuge to the Three Jewels again and again, remembering their good qualities and the differences between them — recognizing their superiority over ordinary worldly forms of refuge. Two, to offer the first portion of whatever we eat or drink to the Three Jewels, remembering their kindness. Three, with our heart full of compassion and mindful of living beings' various capacities, always to encourage others to go for refuge. Four, remembering the benefits of going for refuge, to go for refuge at least three times during the day and three times during the night. Five, to perform every action with complete trust in the Three Jewels, regardless of what situation arises, what frame of mind we're in, and whether or not we're healthy. Finally, six, we should never forsake the Three Jewels, even at the cost of our life or as a joke.”

“The practice of refuge is extremely vast and profound. There is not a single practice in the lesser or greater vehicles of Buddhism that is not included within the refuge taken by beings of various levels of motivation. When the great Indian master Atisha first came to Tibet, he taught widely on the subject of refuge. As a result, the Tibetans jokingly named him the Refuge Lama. When Atisha learned that the Tibetans were referring to him in this way, he was very pleased.”

These are incredible, all six of them. They're really interesting and evocative, and they have a lot of depth. They can be done really simply, but they can also be really challenging in our approach. They're quite nice because they can kind of scale as we put energy into them. They don't ever kind of go dry. They just keep getting richer and richer and more interesting throughout our whole Dharma career.

We can funnel them into our practice. For example, to offer the first portion of whatever we eat or drink to the Three Jewels, remembering their kindness. This is specifically pausing whenever we eat or drink to remember Buddha and how kind Buddha is, and of course how kind the Dharma Jewel is, and the Sangha Jewel. So this is basically remembering our faith in the Three Jewels whenever we eat or drink, which is amazing. This really helps whatever Dharma practice we're working on, because from faith comes everything, and we eat and drink a lot — always sipping on something and nibbling on something. So if we do this every time we eat or drink, we'll be igniting our faith, maybe our faith in the specific thing we're working on, all day, over and over again.

With a heart full of compassion and mindful of living beings' various capacities, always to encourage others to go for refuge. This is about remembering our compassion, which supports every Dharma realization. Compassion becomes fertile ground for any Dharma realization that we're developing. But this vow is also about wishing people to have Dharma — encouraging people to go for refuge, with compassion. Even people who don't necessarily have an explicit practice. Not in a proselytizing way — that's why Geshe-la says, mindful of living beings' various capacities. But you're encouraging them out of compassion to find happiness from within.

Whenever we're meditating on something or working on a little Dharma project, we can think, how wonderful it would be if my friends and family had this insight. And it really helps our own experience of it. Sometimes we're better at wishing for things for others than for ourselves. So like, let's just take seeking to accumulate virtuous actions and not non-virtuous actions, if that's what you want to work on. It's like, wow, wouldn't that be amazing if this friend of mine really wanted to accumulate virtuous actions? Wouldn't that be so beautiful for them, to have this virtuous clarity, this moral clarity in their life? And they just loved creating good karma and abandoning creating bad karma — they just loved moral discipline. Wouldn't that be so wonderful for them? Especially if it's a loved one or someone who's really making a mess of their life. We wish that for that person, and then all of a sudden we start to wish that for ourselves too. That's a little trick. And we want to get experience of it out of our compassion, because we know that will make us a lot more effective at helping them get that experience.

This one is a little bit about teaching Dharma too, and the benefits that come from teaching Dharma, which are explained extensively in Joyful Path of Good Fortune.

Remembering the benefits of going for refuge, to go for refuge at least three times during the day and three times during the night. Every time we go for refuge, we can think, I go for refuge to Dharma, and remember the thing that we're working on. So now we're creating all this mindfulness in the day. It's like getting supported all day, six times at least.

To perform every action with complete trust in the Three Jewels, regardless of what situation arises, what frame of mind we're in, and whether or not we're healthy. That's a huge practice. It's kind of related to what Neil was talking about in the data sharing in the first class — trying to remember the Three Jewels in every action. And that's what makes it meaningful.

Never forsake the Three Jewels, even at the cost of our life, or as a joke. This is having this incredible sacred feeling about the Three Jewels, that they're just beyond the ordinary.

These six practices are also explained in Joyful Path of Good Fortune with quite a bit of detail. If you want to look at some commentary and unpack them in more detail, please do check that.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraph 339: benefits of going for refuge
teaching.text:
Benefits, quickly. There are eight benefits of going for refuge. I remember this by remembering P-E-P-A-H-P-U-Q. Yeah, super helpful. And it spells Peppa Pig. Do you know Peppa Pig? It's an awful cartoon, I think. Oh, it's Peppa Pug, but it's Pig, close enough.

We become a pure Buddhist, or inner being. That's the first P. We establish the foundation for taking all other vows, such as lay, ordained, Bodhisattva, and Tantric vows. That's the E. And we purify the negative karma that we've accumulated in the past. That's the second P. We daily accumulate a vast amount of merit. That's the A. It's like a British person saying it. We're held back from falling into the lower realms. That's the H. We're protected from harm inflicted by humans and non-humans. That's the P in Pug. We fulfill all our temporary and ultimate wishes. That's the U, ultimate. And finally, we quickly attain the full enlightenment of Buddhahood. That's the Q.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Inner being is a fantastic epithet, synonym for Buddhist. Pure Buddhist — inner being. It's just really nice for us all to ask this question: would I describe myself as an inner being? I think this is the only place where Geshe-la uses this exact phrase. The meaning that it points to is very clarifying. Inner being really just means we find our happiness from within and we find our freedom from suffering from within. That's what an inner being is.

With this point about the spiritual path that we're on, we're trying to check which direction am I moving in? It can be a little bit unclear sometimes. I think the last time we checked in as a class was in December — there was a little analogy about a flaming plane, whether we're on the runway, or whether we're getting up, whether we're cruising, whether we're going down, whether we're crashed and burning.

So there's the Five Mahayana Paths, there are the sixteen conceptions. We can kind of check which direction am I moving. It's not that helpful to check in day by day, because it's hard to tell. But on like a three to six month pace, it's somewhat useful. Have I become more of an inner being over these last five months, since December, or less? Basically, have I looked for happiness from within more? Have I looked for freedom from suffering from within more? Or have I looked for happiness outside myself more?

We're never asking these questions out of perfectionism. We're never asking out of judgment, out of attacking ourselves or criticizing ourselves. We're just asking out of a kindness to ourselves — to get some clarity about which direction our path is moving in. Because it's hard to tell with so many facets, this one question is like a somewhat easy question to answer and evaluate. Looks like more, looks like less, or looks like somewhat the same.

If it's more — that we're looking for happiness from within — we can think, that's amazing, I'm so proud, that's perfect. I don't need any more than that. In three months, may I say the same. If it's less, we can think, okay, this is a sign that I need these incontrovertible Dharma understandings. I need more solid understandings in my heart, because there's something a little bit fragile here, something a little bit rocky inside me that's vulnerable to the changing conditions of life. That's okay, but I need to be aware of that. I want to make some changes. This is why I'm going to start working on one of these sixteen conceptions. I can use the commitments of refuge to support that — to be anchors or scaffolding for that.

If someone asks you sometimes, what's a Buddhist, and you feel like it's too complicated to go into the details, you can say: inner being. It's just an inner being.

teaching.speaker: Mimi
teaching.text: Regarding the general commitments of offering the first portion of whatever we eat — what if we're doing that to Vajrayogini? Same thing, right?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yep. It's just a lovely example of how these commitments flow into our tantric practice. In the Vajrayogini practices, we have the eleven yogas. The yoga of eating is in kind of two of them — one is in the yoga of accumulating, or it's actually in three: the yoga of the Guru, the yoga of purifying nectar, and also the yoga of daily actions. It's basically transforming our eating, because it happens so much, and it's one of the main objects of what we look for happiness outside of ourselves.

So it's something to really transform into the complete purity of enjoyment. And yeah, we start working on that when we get the refuge commitments, which again is just so cool. It's like Buddha's leading us into the tantric practices very skillfully, day one. But then when we start practicing tantra, we see how we can do this a little bit more skillfully and elegantly. We're not just eating in a complicated way with this long meditation in mind. We realize, oh, I can offer that to myself as Vajrayogini, or to my Guru at my heart as Vajrayogini Heruka. And that's basically accomplishing the same goal.

Basically all the sutra and tantra always kind of combines like this. Over time, we'll just start to see it's the same. They're just leading in the exact same place, and they're mutually supportive.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, good. Let's have some time for discussion now. Let's do Fran and Sumit and Neil and Anne P.

pairedDiscussion.note: Paired discussion segment removed. Audio was heavily garbled and largely unintelligible in both Whale and Dolphin transcriptions. Participants included Fran, Sumit, Neil, and Anne P. Topics touched on included the challenge of practicing all the commitments in daily life, the discipline of responding to invitations (referencing Anne K's example of always replying), offering food to the Three Jewels and Vajrayogini, and the interplay of faith and fear in refuge practice.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Any specific things we want to do over this next two weeks? Because we're off for Memorial Day weekend. So we'll be back on the 31st.

conclusion.speaker: David
conclusion.text: I was thinking we could pick one of the sixteen things we wanted to work on and try to move from a correct belief to a valid cognizer. And also — sorry, slight tangent. In the first half, I want to make sure there was something that didn't get lost in the recording. You said if we don't have perfect renunciation or bodhichitta, we can like remember the Buddhas, or I forget the exact practice that that was. I thought that might be good too.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Yeah. That point was that there's something called contaminated virtue, which means a virtuous action not done either with renunciation or bodhichitta or perfectly in remembering emptiness. And it's basically virtue that creates good conditions in samsara. So it's hard to create uncontaminated virtue without those minds. And it's hard to generate those minds as the drive behind every action.

But there's one other way to create uncontaminated virtue, which is basically to do it while remembering Buddha, or in relationship to Buddha, because Buddha is outside samsara. So yeah, of course, we can remember Buddha in everything we do. It's a great way to engage in refuge in a very simple but profound way.

conclusion.speaker: Kristin
conclusion.text: So Mimi, Grady, and I all arrived at thinking that happiness can be found in samsara. And so we're going to work on that one and kind of apply it to the Lamrim object of the day and kind of see it from that angle to improve our practice as an inner being.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Yeah, fantastic. I love that all three of you zoomed in on the same one. It's nice. It's like a little sign that it was right for you all. That's a really fun one to just play around with and explore. And the Lamrim will all kind of mutually support that.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text: This Saturday is the first family class. We'll have one a month through the summer, to start, with Miss Mimi. Spread the word if you can. Then the Saturday after that, we'll have a course on the traveler mindset — understanding past and future lives. Very happy about that. And the Saturday after that, we have our Win-Win: Creating a Win-Win World all-day special course. We'll be exploring that on June 6th.

questionAndAnswer.speaker: Sumit
questionAndAnswer.text: So my understanding is that in terms of going back to Mahayana paths, there's five paths. And there's like a difference in the Hinayana practice. Is that correct? There's a little difference in the five?

questionAndAnswer.speaker: Kadam Kyle
questionAndAnswer.text: Well, there definitely is because there's no bodhichitta.

questionAndAnswer.speaker: Sumit
questionAndAnswer.text: I guess I noticed and was like, what's up with that? Why is that? I was wondering if you could talk about that. It's something I've wondered about for a long time.

questionAndAnswer.speaker: Kadam Kyle
questionAndAnswer.note: Extended teaching on Hinayana vs. Mahayana mindsets
questionAndAnswer.text:
So basically, why is there a difference between the Hinayana paths and the Mahayana paths? There's lots of different types of Hinayana being too — returners and once-returners and never-returners and stream-enterers. There's all these different permutations of Hinayana practitioner based on their aim.

Maybe what I can do now with our time is just talk a little bit about this and try to make it practical and helpful. Generally speaking, Buddha taught two types of Dharma — the Hinayana and the Mahayana. The Mahayana can be divided into two: the Vajrayana, which includes all the normal Mahayana paths plus tantra, and then just the general Mahayana. All types of Buddhism are precious and lead to liberation and enlightenment eventually. They're all precious and special in their own way. But Buddha taught this because there are different types of people with different types of karma.

No one really practices the explicit Hinayana paths anymore in this world. Most of these lineages have died out for different reasons. But the Hinayana mindset is something really worth practically considering and thinking about.

The Hinayana mindset is this: it's basically thinking it's too much to attain enlightenment. Full enlightenment is just too big of a deal. Helping all living beings and their karma and their mess is too complicated. What I need to do is attain realization of emptiness so I can become free. We'll figure the rest out later, but that's what I need to do.

The Hinayana approach is therefore to just practice the Three Higher Trainings — moral discipline, concentration, and wisdom. It's like trying to really quickly understand emptiness to have no suffering anymore. That's all I can focus on. It's just too much to become enlightened.

So they spend a lot of time not being around people, not being around things. Generally speaking, people are like an object to be abandoned in the Hinayana because it's too easy to get attached to them, too easy to break your moral discipline, too easy to harm them. A lot of Hinayana practitioners will isolate or be in a monastery — that kind of mindset.

We can hold the Mahayana tenets — like be here, which means hold the Mahayana in our views and our aspirations — but still have Hinayana ways of being. This is where it can be very practical to think about. When we think about our practice, how often do we think it would be nice without all these people around? It's the people that are getting in my way of my practice. That's a little bit of a Hinayana mindset.

Or my solution to my delusion problem is to abandon things and difficult situations. In the short term, that can be helpful. But in the long term, that's really not a Mahayana attitude. The Mahayana attitude is: I transform it into the path. I'm going to be with the people. I'm going to be with the world, but transform my way of thinking.

Or how often do we think, I just want to do my practice and get away from all these annoying people and situations? We use our practice as a little bit like an escape. That's a little bit like the Hinayana attitude.

The Mahayana is like building a palace, and the Hinayana is like building a shack. If you're in a rainstorm, a shack is refuge. You're protected. But it doesn't help anyone else. It's easy to make. It's quick to make. But it just kind of helps you. And it's not too sophisticated in the long run.

A palace is complicated to make. It takes a lot of time, a lot of energy. But you can host countless beings, and it lasts forever. So our own enlightenment, which the Mahayana is aiming for, is like building a palace. What the Hinayana is aiming for is like a shack. It's still great. It's still refuge. It's still completely a pure thing to do. It's also way simpler to do. It takes a lot less tools than to build a marble palace. But the aim is a little bit less.

So practically, it's just nice to have an idea that there's not really anyone holding Hinayana tenets these days. But it's very easy to hold the Hinayana mindset, which is: I'm just worried about my thing, and then I'll deal with all you people later. The Mahayana mindset is more like: no, you are an inextricable part of my journey, my path. I can't have a path, a journey, without all living beings being part of it. And I'm doing this for all of them. And yeah, it's big and complicated sometimes, but I'm building a palace here. I'm not building a shack. I'm building something that's going to last for a very long time — forever.

If you want to know more, Geshe-la does explain bits in the first couple of chapters of Ocean of Nectar about the different types of Hinayana being — the returners, once-returners, stream-enterers, and so on.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: All right, let's dedicate here. You can think through the virtues you've collected, through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment.

dedication.speaker: Grady
dedication.text: You can make any personal prayers or dedications. Okay, thank you. Thanks, everyone.
